blocks.title: Why OWASP LLM Top 10 matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: A security team threat-models an LLM app against prompt injection, data leakage, and tool abuse. The learner's job is not to memorize OWASP LLM Top 10; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved top risks mapped to tests and mitigations.

Running case: OWASP LLM Top 10 threat model for a support assistant. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if classic web checks pass while LLM-specific attack paths remain open, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson assumes you can learn the vocabulary, then spends its effort on integration choices, failure signals, and checks that make the idea usable in a real system.

items.text: Product framing: OWASP LLM Top 10 matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: OWASP LLM Top 10 matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure top risks mapped to tests and mitigations on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: OWASP LLM Top 10 threat model for a support assistant

spans.text: Scenario: A security team threat-models an LLM app against prompt injection, data leakage, and tool abuse. The team wants to improve top risks mapped to tests and mitigations, but it has already seen this failure: classic web checks pass while LLM-specific attack paths remain open.
Here is the worked artifact at design-review depth: concrete enough to inspect, small enough to build as a thin slice.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Launch review: a customer-facing AI feature touches user data, external tools, or regulated decisions. The team needs a risk classification and controls before it ships.

Artifact: OWASP LLM Top 10 threat model for a support assistant. It maps data flows, user harms, threat scenarios, required controls, human review, logging, and the release evidence for top risks mapped to tests and mitigations.
Worked output: classify the feature, identify sensitive data, block unsafe tool use, add audit logging, test a misuse case, and assign an owner for unresolved risk.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: AI safety reviewer. Context: A security team threat-models an LLM app against prompt injection, data leakage, and tool abuse. Task: complete a risk review for OWASP LLM Top 10 threat model for a support assistant. Include data handled, user harm, tool risk, misuse test, mitigation, owner, and release decision. Output: {risk_category, controls, tests, unresolved_risks, owner}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties OWASP LLM Top 10 to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

spans.text: Mechanism opens the machinery behind OWASP LLM Top 10. In the running case, the important question is: what exactly changes between the user's request and the final output?
Mechanism means mapping data, users, tools, threats, controls, and accountability before launch.

Technical framing: imagine a trace. It should expose inputs, state, external evidence, model or algorithm output, validation result, and owner for exceptions.

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: classic web checks pass while LLM-specific attack paths remain open. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to OWASP LLM Top 10 threat model for a support assistant: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: top risks mapped to tests and mitigations becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful OWASP LLM Top 10 design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: classic web checks pass while LLM-specific attack paths remain open. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: A policy exists in prose but is not enforced at the tool, data, or release boundary.
The system passes benign tests but follows instructions embedded in untrusted content.
Sensitive data is minimized in the app but retained in logs or traces.
The broad warning sign: top risks mapped to tests and mitigations gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.

capstone.prompt: Create a one-page release-ready plan for OWASP LLM Top 10 threat model for a support assistant. Include: the user problem, realistic input, mechanism, design choice, runnable or reviewable check, metric (top risks mapped to tests and mitigations), failure case (classic web checks pass while LLM-specific attack paths remain open), owner, and the next rung after this lesson.
